newsitem.title: FRANCE: Trichet makes classic deficit cut call - economists.
newsitem.headline: Trichet makes classic deficit cut call - economists.

text.p: French economists said Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet delivered a "classic" and unsurprising message on Tuesday on the need to keep cutting public deficits.
The timing of the message was important, however, given the change of government since the left-wing election victory on June 1, they said.
"The speech is more or less the same as last year -- it was strongly centred on a need for deficit reduction," said Deutsche Bank economist Patrick Mange.

"The tenor was clearly that less deficits are a condition for growth, and in particular structural deficit reduction. Another important message was that you have to take care on public payrolls," Mange said.
Eric Muller, Paris-based economist at UBS said Trichet's news conference on the Bank of France's annual report carried no surprises, but was clearly well-timed.
"One of the points in relations between the central bank and the government has been a sort of agreement on loosening monetary policy in exchange for a relatively strict budget policy," he said.
"I think what Trichet said implicitly was that the current conditions of monetary policy are consistent with the pursuit of deficit reduction and public spending reduction," he said.
"It was his role to say that current conditions, for example short-term interest rates, are stimulative and compensate fiscal tightening," Muller said.
"I think what he (Trichet) said today is 'I am recalling the conditions of this policy mix'".
"There are very few chances of the Bank of France taking a hostile reaction to (government) policy in the coming months," he said.
"It was his duty to spell out the Bank's policy. It was a classic intervention, the tone was relatively firm."
Trichet, whose presentation of the central bank's annual report for 1996 was delayed due to the June 1 election, said public deficit reduction and structural reform were crucial for economic growth.
He also said business investment was the weak point in the economy, not consumer spending.
Trichet also said he expected the euro single currency to start on time on January 1, 1999, and that this was a commitment made by new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin which he fully shared.
He said he believed France, Germany and Italy would take any necessary steps to correct deficits in line with the needs for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
